Messages.Author: quetzalcoatl
Messages.Body:
Actually here in Australia (where Sutekh is from ) cheese is any play
that relies on nothing more than just playing the cards as they come -
no tactics, no style.

So for example a Stealth/Bleed deck is cheese because you just tap the
vampires, bleed at stealth for massive amounts, rinse and repeat. We
rate them (and their smelliness) based on if they even bother with
combat defence or just bleed, die, bring out a new minion, bleed, die,
etc.

And so even though he seems to have reworded the term to the US
contingents, in Australia it is used in a different context - our
parlance is not the same.

D

>combat discipline and a way to get into combat, and then drawing cards
>to make it go? Or a vote deck, which generally has political actions, a
>discipline to pass votes, and drawing cards to make it go?

On this point, it's things like this that mean it's often worthwhile
getting players to play a deck before dismissing it as "cheesy",
"sleazy", "boring", "easy", "over-powered" or whatever other terms
people throw at decks they don't happen to like.

If you look at, say, some trick decks, something like Turbo Arika or
Turbo Baron is often the sort of deck that people abuse as being <some
term of abuse>. But when you actually sit down and play such decks, or
stand over someone's shoulder and watch all the decisions they're having
to make, it can be a LOT less simple. They're not drawing what they
should (or at least what they hope), because their deck has clumped as
any randomly shuffled deck can. Or a particularly unfortunate
combination of cards has transpired to mean that the holes in their deck
- which most such decks have in spades, if you can get in under the
covers - can be exposed but it doesn't want to draw attention to them.
And the general table wrath issues, on top of anything else.

And that, of course, extends to many, many deck types. Rush combat,
say. Do I attempt this rush now, when I don't quite have the cards I
need in hand BUT there's a reasonable chance I can draw them? Say I
have a Bum's Rush, a Flash, a Torn Signpost and a Sideslip on hand - but
I don't have a Blur or an Immortal Grapple. If I rush now and screw it
up, things could go badly. If I don't rush now, he might be able to
oust me next turn if he has a bleed modifier (of which there are a
scattering, but not lots, in his ash heap).

Similarly, stealth bleed decks can often find themselves in trouble
against combat decks, table wrath, bounce and so on. If I go all out
NOW, I can probably get that VP. But if I go all out and dump 12 bleed
in one turn, it's opening me up to a lot of problems with Deflection and
those people cross-table who were turning a blind eye to me will
suddenly think "What the hell?" and start helping out.

>I suspect that James was not actually trying to figure out the
>defenition of "cheese", any more than I am, but was instead questioning
>the very concept as silly. But I could be wrong.

Sort of. There's also the fact that any deck which is somehow an "abuse
of the rules", or somesuch, is something that should be addressed and
remedied if it actually is an abuse of the rules, rather than a deck-
style that just isn't liked by some people. (Pretty much every deck-
style isn't liked by some people.) Or where thinking "Hey, this is a
game that's going to have a lot of <some popular or brand new
technology> in it, so I'll actually think about that when building my
deck" is somehow considered an "abuse of the rules", because that means
you can't think "Hey, I might see quite a few Laibon" when Legacies of
Blood gets released (which would be strange).

In as much as that sort of thing doesn't make a whole lot of sense, it
doesn't make a whole lot more sense to start deciding that cheese and
sleaze suddenly mean brand new nonsensical things.



Dave, I'm not quite sure I follow your angle (or more to the point, I'm
not sure if your angle is dicky or not...) Yes. Rush decks (all Rush
decks, mono discipline weenie or no) require a great deal of table
management and careful play to be successful with. But so do vote
decks. And S+B decks. So on one hand, *all* deck archetypes require
analysis and deliberate play. On the other hand, all decks are designed
to do something, and as long as you draw cards, you can pretty much do
that thing.

In terms of the discussion that was at hand at the time (i.e. "cheesy"
decks or something), all decks are essentially the same--your deck does
something, and as long as you draw cards and nothing foils you, it is
going to do that:

-S+B: Draw cards to bleed at stealth. As long as you draw cards, your
vampires aren't all killed, and your prey can't block/bounce your
bleeds, you'll do ok.

-Vote: Draw cards to call votes. As long as you draw cards, your
vampires aren't all killed, and your prey can't block or vote down your
votes, you'll do ok.

-Rush: Draw cards to kill people. As long as you draw cards, your
vampires aren't all killed, and your prey can't foil your combat,
you'll do ok.

*All* decks are "point and go". And all decks require careful table
management and selective action to do well with. Which was my point.

I'm still kinda lost on yours.

-Peter

I was thinking some about this sort of thing at work earlier, and your
post reminded me of it.

At a very highly skilled level (e.g. if you took the best five players
in the world and made them fight it out), most solid decks would require
a heck of a lot of skill to play.

When you move further down the skill level, generally speaking it's much
easier to oust a newbie if you have a bleed deck, or a vote deck. The
skill level needed for a combat deck drops too, but there's still quite
a few decisions you need to make that don't vary as much from the top
rank games - you still have some pretty precarious decisions to make
about when to back-rush and when to pile in on your prey, and whether to
skip forward to tenderise your grand-prey or not, and so on.

I'm not quite sure where I'm going with this, it's just a thought that
occurred while I was bored. But maybe "cheese" (whatever that might be)
is related to how easy the deck is when playing against easy prey - a
deck that has more effort required at that level is inherently less
cheesy, perhaps.

All decks aren't the same. I mean, we can just forego trying to nail

The difference is that Rush can be foiled by a simple choice. Your
prey can choose to not bring out any vampires, in which case he drags

choice is largely what I was talking about (along with the backoust

have a horde of weenies who can bleed for one. But if you don't, pure
rush is going to be *very* difficult. You can certainly hybrid your
deck, and probably should, but that doesn't change the truth of what
I'm saying. And also note that the other two won't *require*
hybridization. These are some of the reasons I'm willing to assert
(non-weenie) rush is more difficult to play. You could also just count
up the number of rush decks, bleed decks, and vote decks in the TWD
archive and support the assertion that way, but it's a different line
of argument than the one I'm making now.

All decks aren't equally so. We may have just reached the
Bakija-Cherryholmes Point of Dueling Assertions.

Messages.Author: firstco...@aol.com
Messages.Body:
pd...@lightlink.com wrote:
> bluedevil wrote:
> > All decks aren't the same. I mean, we can just forego trying to nail
> > down what "cheesy" is and, as long as we can agree that it is
> > *something*, then I would say some decks possess that quality in
> > greater amounts than others. Hence, all decks are clearly not the
> > same.
>
> Yeah, see, I am unwilling to agree that "cheesy" means anything at all

Some decks do not permit much player interaction (outside of ganging up
on the deck itself). Other decks ruin the spirit of the format or
change entirely the game you are playing. In my experience, these are
almost always the only decks called "cheesy" or "sleazy".

A deck which relies entirely on Obedience and master cards is an
example of the former. You'll never use any intercept to stop its
actions as it doesn't take any. You'll never rush it successfully
unless it somehow runs out of Obedience.

Bringing a Merge Sebastian Goulet deck to a NoR prerelease is an
example of the latter--why have a prerelease? To use the new cards.
Why bring disincentive to use the new cards? Cause it wins. Why win
if noone's enjoying themselves? Dunno.

I think these two concepts have been equivocated accidentally in this
thread. If your playgroup is not getting to experience the new cards
during a prerelease, maybe you've outgrown your format, or maybe some
players just don't understand the point of the format to be the same
thing. HOWEVER, if a deck in Vampire is able to be a Solitaire deck,
then there's a problem.

In my recollection, the only real approaching-solitaire V:TES deck was
the Anarch Revolt Parthenon Anson monstrosity, which just might oust
you before you can burn even 1 of its Revolts--but that's fixed now.
Stealth bleed is "non interactive" in the sense that if you're not
playing rush, and you can't catch their gobs of stealth, and you aren't
playing bounce, then you're going to lose 5-10 pool a turn until you
die, and there's nothing you can do about it. These things are
considerations for deck design, and really, stealth bleed is so
incredibly powerfully solitaire in its style that it has to be planned
for-- and it's so planned for that it's standard to include 8 copies of
Deflection in your deck. Which makes it not solitaire anymore.

Just posting to increase understanding. I hope you've learned
something from this post, Peter, and if you disagree with me, then I
hope I will learn something from your post.

-- Brian
